questions.stem: Fibrillations and positive sharp waves are often seen on electromyography in which of the following neuromuscular junction disorders?
questions.stemHtml: Fibrillations and positive sharp waves are often seen on electromyography in which of the following neuromuscular junction disorders?

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Botulism: Of the options listed, botulism is the only one that results in fibrillations and positive sharp waves (usually within 4-5 days of onset of neurologic symptoms) and is categorized as a neuromuscular junction disorder. While fibrillations and positive sharp waves are not typical findings in MG, they may be seen in other neuromuscular conditions. In MG, the characteristic electrophysiological findings include decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation and increased jitter on single fiber electromyography (SFEMG). Option B - Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder in which autoantibodies target voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) at the presynaptic terminal of the neuromuscular junction. Fibrillations and positive sharp waves are not common features of LEMS. Instead, the characteristic electrophysiological finding in LEMS is an improvement in muscle strength following repetitive nerve stimulation due to the increased release of acetylcholine caused by the autoantibodies' effect on VGCCs. Option C - Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome due to a COLQ Mutation: Congenital myasthenic syndromes (CMS) are a group of genetic disorders that affect neuromuscular transmission. Mutations in various genes can lead to different subtypes of CMS. The electrophysiological findings in CMS may include a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation or abnormalities on single fiber electromyography (SFEMG). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following genes is not linked to autosomal recessive Parkinson disease?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following genes is not linked to autosomal recessive Parkinson disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - MAPT: PRKN, PINK1, and DJ-1 mutations cause early-onset, autosomal recessive Parkinson disease. MAPT encodes the protein tau, and patients with mutations in this gene may develop parkinsonism in association with frontotemporal dementia. Alterations in MAPT have also been associated with Pick Disease, Alzheimer disease, argyrophilic grain disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, and corticobasal degeneration. The tau protein is implicated as a modifier of disease phenotype in idiopathic Parkinson disease; however, mutations in MAPT are not associated with autosomal recessive, early onset Parkinson disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - PRKN (Parkin): Mutations in the PRKN gene are associated with autosomal recessive juvenile Parkinson's disease (also known as Parkin-linked Parkinson's disease). This form of Parkinson's disease typically has an early onset and is characterized by a lack of response to levodopa treatment. Option B - PINK1: Mutations in the PINK1 gene are associated with autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease. PINK1 encodes a protein involved in mitochondrial quality control, and mutations in this gene can lead to mitochondrial dysfunction and contribute to the development of Parkinson's disease. Option C - DJ-1: Mutations in the DJ-1 gene are also associated with autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease. DJ-1 is involved in protecting cells from oxidative stress, and mutations can disrupt cellular mechanisms that help maintain cell health. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy is newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis based on skin findings, family history, and genetic testing, but is otherwise normal. At what time would a brain MRI be recommended?
questions.stemHtml: A 14-month-old boy is newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis based on skin findings, family history, and genetic testing, but is otherwise normal. At what time would a brain MRI be recommended?

options.label: B
options.text: Defer until abnormal neurological exam findings

options.label: C
options.text: Perform when developmental delay is apparent or following his first seizure

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Soon after diagnosis: Brain MRI with and without contrast should be performed when the diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis is made, to screen for subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA). Although these are benign tumors, they can hemorrhage or grow rapidly, so surgical resection or treatment with an mTOR inhibitor (everolimus) is recommended after identification of a SEGA. Other brain lesions that can be assessed by MRI include cortical tubers, migrational defects, and subependymal nodules. Incorrect Options: Option B - Defer until abnormal neurological exam findings: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder characterized by the growth of numerous noncancerous (benign) tumors in multiple organs, including the brain. While it's true that some individuals with TSC may remain asymptomatic or have mild symptoms, brain involvement can occur without obvious neurological findings. Early detection of brain lesions, such as subependymal nodules and cortical tubers, can be crucial for appropriate management and intervention, even in the absence of overt neurological symptoms. Option C - Perform when developmental delay is apparent or following his first seizure: While waiting for developmental delay or the occurrence of a seizure to perform a brain MRI might capture some cases of brain involvement, it's important to note that brain lesions associated with TSC can be present before obvious symptoms develop. Early imaging can help identify lesions that may require monitoring and intervention, allowing for better management of the condition. Option D - Prior to onset of puberty: While it's important to continue monitoring individuals with TSC throughout their lifetime, waiting until puberty to perform a brain MRI may result in delayed identification of brain lesions that could potentially require early intervention. Brain lesions associated with TSC can occur at any age, and early detection is valuable for appropriate management. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which cell type, infected by HIV in the central nervous system, is thought to provide a latent reservoir for the virus to allow for “viral escape”?
questions.stemHtml: Which cell type, infected by HIV in the central nervous system, is thought to provide a latent reservoir for the virus to allow for “viral escape”?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Microglia: HIV primarily infects macrophages/microglial cells of the CNS, as well as astrocytes, unlike outside the CNS where it primarily infects CD4+ T-lymphocytes. HIV does not destroy these microglia but does remain active and continues to replicate in these cells, some of which form multinucleated giant cells. Infected astrocytes often contain dormant virus. Both of these cells provide a “reservoir” for the virus in the CSF and are believed to play an important role in the concept of “viral escape” of the virus into the CNS. This phenomenon also likely contributes to the fact that HAND and progressive atrophy persist in the post-ART era. Incorrect Options: Option A- Oligodendroglia: Oligodendroglia are a type of glial cell that produces myelin in the central nervous system (CNS). While they are involved in myelination and maintenance of nerve fibers, they are not known to be a primary target for HIV infection. The primary targets of HIV in the CNS are immune cells. Option C- CD4+ Lymphocytes: CD4+ T lymphocytes are immune cells that express the CD4 receptor, which HIV uses to gain entry into cells. In the central nervous system, CD4+ lymphocytes can be infected by HIV, leading to viral replication and inflammation. However, they are not considered the primary latent reservoir for the virus in the CNS. Option D- CD8+ Lymphocytes: CD8+ T lymphocytes are another type of immune cell that plays a role in immune responses. They are primarily responsible for targeting and killing infected cells. While CD8+ lymphocytes can interact with and respond to HIV-infected cells, they are not considered the primary target for HIV infection in the CNS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Move to angiography suite for CT angiography of brain to look for aneurysm: This patient has a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and needs an urgent evaluation by CT angiography of the brain. Symptoms of SAH include headache (48%), dizziness (10%), orbital pain (7%), diplopia (4%), and visual loss (4%). Physical examination findings may be normal or may include mild to moderate BP elevation, temperature elevation, tachycardia, papilledema, retinal hemorrhage, and global or focal neurologic abnormalities. Complications of SAH include hydrocephalus, rebleeding, vasospasm, seizures, and cardiac dysfunction. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Schwann cells: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) involves progressive demyelination of the peripheral nervous system . Schwann cells produce the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system. GBS frequently occurs following inflammatory, bloody diarrhea due to Campylobacter jejuni and is more common in patients with pre-existing autoimmune diseases. The clinical presentation involves progressive sensory deficits and weakness, usually beginning in the lower extremities in a stocking-and-glove distribution as it moves toward the upper extremities. Physical examination indicates peripheral nerve deficits, including hyporeflexia. The diagnosis is assisted by lumbar puncture demonstrating albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with a normal white blood cell count) and a nerve conduction study (NCS). NCS and needle electromyography evaluate the electrical properties of peripheral nerves with externally applied stimuli and analysis of the subsequent neurologic response. Recordings can help differentiate between primary nerve and muscle disorders and delineate the site of neuronal dysfunction. NCS results consistent with myelin degeneration (as in GBS) show markedly slowed conduction velocities or absent responses, as well as prolonged distal motor latency, since myelin allows the rapid transmission of action potentials along the axon. Conduction abnormalities progress over time, so serial NCS testing may be useful. Incorrect Options: Option A - Oligodendrocytes: Oligodendrocytes provide the myelin sheath for axons in the central nervous system (CNS). Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating process that occurs in the CNS, but NCS does not have a role in diagnosis of that disease. Option C - Axon: NCS consistent with axonal degeneration would result in a reduced amplitude and an increased dispersion. Velocity may be minimally reduced but not to the degree of myelin degeneration. Option D - Skeletal muscle fibers: NCS of myopathies varies but typically reveals decreased amplitudes.
